units.text: You'll learn how to reach a private bucket, authorize encrypted reads, and recover an earlier version. Start with the application: an S three access point gives it a named S three policy boundary. A V P C endpoint gives it a network path. Those are different jobs.

The application can use the gateway endpoint through a V P C route table, or use the interface endpoint's PrivateLink addresses where the connectivity design calls for them. Neither route grants object access. Check the endpoint, access-point, and bucket policies separately. For example, a route can reach S three successfully while a policy still denies reading the requested key.

Follow the client to S three over H T T P S. That protects data in transit. The object is encrypted at rest: S three manages the key for S S E S three, while S S E K M S adds a K M S key and its own authorization boundary.

Suppose a reader has get object but cannot decrypt the S S E K M S object. The request still fails. Check the effective permission to decrypt with that key, not just the bucket policy. Plan the same independent key access for replication and recovery.

Follow report dot C S V through three changes. Upload creates version one. Overwrite creates version two without removing version one. Delete without a version I D makes a delete marker current, so an ordinary read no longer returns the report.

To restore the latest report, remove the delete marker. To retrieve an older revision, use its version I D. Deleting that specific version is different: it removes that version. Lifecycle can expire old versions; suspending versioning alone does not erase them.

You'll learn how to retain a protected version, serve private content at the edge, and choose an online storage class. Start with retention: governance can be bypassed only with the required permission and explicit request. Compliance cannot be shortened or bypassed before expiry, even by root.

The two controls converge on the same object version. A legal hold has no expiry date. An authorized caller must remove it; the retention date is independent. If both are in effect, lifting the hold does not end the retention period. If the retention date passes first, the hold can still protect the version.

Follow the viewer's H T T P S request to CloudFront. A cache hit is served from the edge; a miss reaches the S three origin. Origin Access Control lets CloudFront sign that origin request, and the bucket policy grants access to the intended distribution.

Keep direct bucket access private and test both routes: the distribution works, the direct unauthorized S three request fails. Use a regular S three bucket origin for O A C, not a website endpoint. Send dynamic application traffic to its own backend. Origin protection is not viewer authorization; if viewers need restricted access, apply that control separately.

All three classes offer millisecond access. Standard fits frequent reads. Standard-I A keeps data across Availability Zones for infrequent access, but adds retrieval charges and minimum billing. One Zone-I A has a different resilience boundary: one Availability Zone.

If you cannot recreate the only copy, don't save money by putting it in One Zone-I A. It cannot survive loss of that Zone. For recreatable data or another durable copy, compare the retrieval charges and the thirty-day, 128-kilobyte billing minima. If the data is rarely read but must withstand the loss of a Zone, choose Standard-I A instead.

You'll learn how to choose an archive tier by recovery time, handle changing read patterns, and expire the right object versions. Start with one archived object. Glacier Instant Retrieval is readable in milliseconds without a restore. Flexible Retrieval requires a restore before you read.

If an investigation needs the object immediately, the instant option meets the timing. If recovery can wait, compare Flexible Retrieval's restore options with Deep Archive's longer lead time. Instant and Flexible have ninety-day minimum storage durations; Deep Archive has one hundred eighty days. Price cannot make up for a missed recovery objective.

With Intelligent-Tiering, follow one eligible object from Frequent Access to Infrequent Access after thirty idle days, then to Archive Instant Access after ninety. Those automatic access tiers still allow immediate reads. An access brings the object back to Frequent Access.

Only enable the optional asynchronous archive tiers when a restore delay is acceptable. Their inactivity thresholds differ, and the object need not pass through every tier. Objects smaller than 128 kilobytes stay in Frequent Access without monitoring; eligible monitored objects have an automation fee.

Lifecycle rules act on different parts of the object's history. For example, a rule can transition the current copy of a report, while another ages out its prior versions. In a versioned bucket, expiring the current version can leave a delete marker instead of removing the old bytes.

Use a prefix or tag filter to scope the rule, not a physical folder. Review old versions, and remove expired delete markers only when eligible. Before activating a rule, check minimum durations, small-object cost, and supported transitions; a rule that moves data sooner is not automatically cheaper.

You'll learn how to choose a replica destination, recover missed objects, and trigger downstream work. First, follow the source bucket's versions. Same-Region Replication can create a separate copy in the same Region. Cross-Region Replication targets another Region when recovery or policy needs geographic separation.

Both buckets need versioning, and an I A M role performs replication. For eligible S S E K M S objects, configure replication for those objects and authorize its keys. Copying an object version does not copy the source bucket's whole configuration.

A live replication rule handles eligible new versions. For example, if the source already has yesterday's objects, use S three Batch Replication for the existing set or to repair gaps. S three Replication Time Control applies to eligible live replication, not to a batch backfill.

Delete markers can replicate only when supported and configured; deleting a specific source version does not perform the same delete on the destination. Test which deletes and delays your recovery design tolerates before making the replica your recovery copy.

Start with the bucket event, such as a new invoice. A prefix of invoices slash and a suffix of dot CSV narrow the keys that match; the suffix is not an arbitrary wildcard. Then grant delivery to the chosen Lambda function, Standard S Q S queue or Standard S N S topic.

The upload and notification handling are separate. A notification can arrive again or out of order, so verify the relevant key and version where applicable before updating the business record. If a Lambda function writes output to the same bucket, keep its output outside the input filter to avoid a loop.

You'll learn how to route S three events and scale both requests and large uploads. Start by enabling S three delivery to EventBridge. The rule matches event fields such as the bucket name and object key; it can send matching work to a queue, a Lambda function, or a state machine.

For the file shown, match the intended bucket and key. A queue gives the worker a backlog, while a state machine can coordinate steps. The rule does not make processing exactly once; set target permissions, handle delivery failures, and make the consumer safe to repeat.

S three scales request rate by partitioned prefix. The images, logs, and reports examples show independent access paths rather than directory servers. The documented baseline is at least three thousand five hundred write-type operations or five thousand five hundred get and HEAD requests per second per partitioned prefix.

Scale gradually; a new traffic pattern can temporarily return five oh three Slow Down. Retry with backoff, but check the client, network and K M S limits too. Spreading requests cannot help if the bottleneck is an independent key-service quota or the client's own connections.

A multipart upload begins with an upload I D. Send numbered parts in parallel and save each part's E tag. If part two fails, retry that part rather than the whole object. Then send the ordered list of part numbers and E tags to complete it. Only completion makes the new object available.

Abort a multipart upload that will not finish, and account for any parts still in flight. Add lifecycle cleanup for abandoned uploads so stored parts don't keep accruing charges. The completed multipart E tag is not necessarily a file checksum; verify integrity using a supported checksum.
